Transporting Wet Paintings

September 28, 2026September 28, 2026 by Dan Scott 13 Comments
September 28, 2026 13
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:46
Instaread

This follows on from my last post: Plein Air Painting With Elora. (Thanks for all the kind words on this post. It means a lot. Chontele and I read some of them out to Elora. She was chuffed.)

As I wrote in that post, Elora and I each created a plein air painting in New Zealand. Mine turned out alright, and Elora’s is precious. But in packing for this trip, I didn’t think about how I would get the paintings home safely. I packed a wet-carry case, but it only fits 5 by 7 inch paintings. Elora’s and my paintings are 9 by 12 inches. I couldn’t wait for them to dry, as they were painted in the last few days of the trip, and the cold weather slowed the drying time of the oil paints. I had to somehow get them home while they were still wet.

My solution was to brace the paintings against each other with a gap between them so the paint wouldn’t smudge. Chontele went out and got clothesline pegs and rubber bands. I placed these pegs around the edges of each painting. Then I stacked the paintings so they faced each other.

I used the rubber bands to secure them together. (You’ll notice there are three gessobords in the photo. I had a spare and stacked it on top of Elora’s painting, which had particularly thick and luscious strokes.)

Then I placed the paintings in the corner of my suitcase, covered them with an old towel, and prayed. I also made sure the bag was full so it wouldn’t move around in there during transit.

It wasn’t the neatest approach, but it worked! Both paintings arrived safely in Brisbane, Australia.

Part of the art life is being resourceful and making do with what you have. Even back in the studio, I often need to slap together odds and ends to get things the way I like it.

I’m sure there are better solutions so don’t feel you need to copy this. But if you have no other options, it’s worth a try.

Also, tomorrow we will be opening our Color Masterclass for enrollment. We only do this twice or so each year to give students the best experience. More details to come if interested.

Happy painting!

Dan Scott

    Dan, I keep a baggie of wine corks cut into 1/3 inch rings and then into half. I cut them with a steak knife. The small cork half-moons do their job. Then just touch up any edge smudges at home. The edges are mostly under a frame eventually anyway.

    I transport paintings by slicing old corks from wine bottles. I then cut these in half, so that the flat side can lie along the outer edge of a painting. I carry the corks in a small bag with my plein air stuff. They are light and don’t take up much room.
